props.title: People
props.sub: grow them, or manage them out

props.title: Growing an engineer to the next level
props.q: Tell me about a time you helped an engineer grow.

moves.title: Set a concrete bar
moves.desc: Name the specific gap between where they were and the next level.

moves.title: Create the reps
moves.desc: Hand them a stretch project with real scope, then step back.

moves.title: Coach, don't rescue
moves.desc: Weekly one-on-ones on the how; let them own the mistakes.

moves.title: Show the promotion
moves.desc: End on the outcome: promoted, or leading what they couldn't before.

props.trap: “I told them to do better and they improved.” No plan, no proof.
props.signal: You build people deliberately, and can scale yourself through others.
props.foot: Growth stories are the most under-prepared, and the most predictive of a good manager.

props.title: Growing an engineer to senior — a full answer
props.situation: On a payments platform doing forty million transactions a day, I had a mid-level engineer, Priya. Technically excellent, but she'd been passed over for senior twice, and she was frustrated.
props.task: My mandate: get her to the senior bar within a year — for real, without lowering it.

actions.d: Wrote the exact gap down with her — it was scope and influence, not coding — mapped to our senior rubric.
Handed her the payment-retry idempotency redesign: cross-team, high-stakes, and I deliberately stayed out of it.
Coached the how in weekly one-on-ones — design reviews, stakeholder pushback — but she made every call.
Created visibility: she presented the design to the org, and I pre-wired the promotion committee.

props.learning: Define the gap in writing on day one. Vague growth goals grow no one.
props.foot: Every action is “I did” — but it ends on her growth, not mine. That's the balance.

props.title: Handling an underperformer
props.q: How did you handle an engineer who was underperforming?

moves.title: Diagnose first
moves.desc: Skill, will, or fit? Each needs a different fix, so don't guess.

moves.title: Make it explicit
moves.desc: Clear expectations, in writing, with dates. No surprises.

moves.title: Support, then decide
moves.desc: Real coaching and a fair runway, then act either way.

moves.title: Protect the team
moves.desc: One tolerated low performer taxes everyone around them.

props.trap: “They weren't good enough, so I let them go.” No diagnosis, no support.
props.signal: You're fair and direct, and you don't avoid hard conversations.
props.foot: They want to see compassion and a spine. Most candidates show only one.

props.title: Turning around an underperformer — a full answer
props.situation: On an ads-ranking team, a solid mid-level engineer, David, had missed his commitments for a full quarter. His code reviews were slow and the team had started to notice.
props.task: My mandate: turn it around fairly within a quarter, or make a clear call.

actions.d: Diagnosed privately first — it wasn't skill. A new baby at home, and he felt his work had gone invisible.
Set explicit written expectations: three concrete deliverables over six weeks, with dates.
Rebalanced his load and gave him a latency project matched to his real strength.
Checked in weekly and documented everything, so there were no surprises for him or me.

props.learning: Diagnose before you judge. Most “underperformance” is context, not capacity.
props.foot: Compassion and a spine in the same story. That's exactly the balance they score.

props.title: Delivering hard feedback
props.q: Tell me about a difficult piece of feedback you gave.

moves.title: Pick real stakes
moves.desc: Choose feedback that was genuinely hard. Behavior, not a typo.

moves.title: Specific and kind
moves.desc: Name the exact behavior and its impact, not their character.

moves.title: Make it a dialogue
moves.desc: Ask for their view; agree on one concrete change together.

moves.title: Follow the thread
moves.desc: Show what changed after. Feedback with no follow-up is venting.

props.trap: You picked a trivial example, or softened it until there was no message.
props.signal: You have the uncomfortable conversation early, before it becomes a crisis.
props.foot: Candor delivered with care is the single most-tested manager skill.

props.title: The brilliant engineer nobody wanted to work with
props.situation: I had a staff engineer, Marco — technically the best on the team. But he was condescending in reviews and meetings, and two engineers had quietly asked to transfer off his projects.
props.task: My mandate: keep his output, fix the behavior, or I'd lose the rest of the team.

actions.d: Gathered specifics first — exact quotes from reviews and meetings, not a vague vibe.
Had a direct, private conversation: named the behavior and its impact on attrition, not his character.
Made it two-way — asked what was driving it; he felt others shipped sloppy work. We agreed on two concrete changes.
Followed up weekly, and deliberately caught him doing it right and reinforced it.

props.learning: Talent never excuses a toxic tax. Address it early, and be specific, not general.
props.foot: Specific, kind, two-way, with follow-up. That's the whole feedback muscle in one story.

props.title: Letting someone go
props.q: Tell me about a time you had to let someone go.

moves.title: Own the context
moves.desc: Briefly: performance or role fit. Never gossip about the person.

moves.title: Show the runway
moves.desc: What you tried first: feedback, a plan, a fair chance.

moves.title: Act with dignity
moves.desc: Decisive, humane, by the book. Protect their exit, not just yours.

moves.title: Carry the lesson
moves.desc: Earlier feedback? A better hire? Show you learned from it.

props.trap: You sound cavalier about firing, or you dodged it until HR forced you.
props.signal: You'll make the hard call, and you'll make it like a human.
props.foot: They're checking you won't keep a bad situation alive out of fear.

props.title: When a good person can't scale with the platform
props.situation: I had an engineer, Sam, eight years tenured and genuinely loved by the team. But we'd moved to large-scale distributed systems, his skills hadn't kept up, and he was now blocking projects.
props.task: My mandate: resolve it — humanely, and without pretending it wasn't happening.

actions.d: Gave honest feedback and a real development plan — training, pairing, a scoped role — over two quarters.
Was explicit about the bar and the risk. No false comfort that things were fine.
When it wasn't closing, I partnered with HR early and arranged a dignified exit with severance and a strong reference.
Protected his dignity — he told the team himself, on his own terms.

props.learning: Kindness is clarity early, not avoidance that ends in a cliff.
props.foot: You made the call, and you made it like a human. That's exactly the signal.

props.title: Conflict
Two engineers at war
props.q: Two of your engineers strongly disagree. What do you do?

moves.title: Get underneath it
moves.desc: Talk to each privately; find the real interest, not the position.

moves.title: Reframe to a shared goal
moves.desc: Anchor both on the outcome they actually both want.

moves.title: Decide if they can't
moves.desc: Facilitate a decision, and make the call yourself if needed.

moves.title: Repair the relationship
moves.desc: The goal isn't a winner; it's two people who work together tomorrow.

props.trap: You took a side, or you let it fester hoping it would resolve itself.
props.signal: You de-escalate, stay neutral, and can still make a decision.
props.foot: The test: is the team calmer or tenser after you get involved?

props.title: Two staff engineers, deadlocked for weeks
props.situation: Two of my staff engineers had been deadlocked for weeks over a new notifications system — one wanted synchronous, one wanted asynchronous. The team was paralyzed and quietly picking sides.
props.task: My mandate: unblock the decision without either of them becoming an enemy.

actions.d: Met each privately — the real fears were different: one feared latency, the other feared operational complexity. Both valid.
Reframed around the shared goal in a joint doc: reliability at scale, with the actual requirements written down.
Ran a time-boxed bake-off with success criteria they both signed off on beforehand.
The data pointed to async; I made the final call publicly, and credited both of them by name.

props.learning: Conflict is usually two right people optimizing different things. Surface the interest.
props.foot: Neutral, structured, decisive — and the relationship survived. That's the whole test.

props.title: Disagreeing with leadership
props.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.

moves.title: Pick a real one
moves.desc: Something that mattered, not the color of a button.

moves.title: Disagree with data
moves.desc: Bring evidence and user or business impact, not just opinion.

moves.title: Commit once decided
moves.desc: Say it clearly, then disagree and commit, and mean it.

moves.title: Know when you're wrong
moves.desc: Bonus points if the leader was right, and you say so.

props.trap: You were a pushover, or you undermined the decision afterward.
props.signal: You have a spine, and you can be an adult about losing a call.
props.foot: They want someone who tells them the truth, then rows in one direction.

props.title: Pushing back on a date that would ship broken
props.situation: My director wanted to commit to a hard external launch date for a checkout redesign, tied to a marketing campaign. I believed it was about six weeks too aggressive and would ship broken.
props.task: My mandate: push back honestly, without becoming the blocker in the room.

actions.d: Didn't argue in the meeting — I came back with data: a bottom-up estimate, the top risk areas, and our QA gap.
Proposed an alternative, not just an objection: a phased rollout that still hit the marketing beat with a smaller scope.
Stated my view clearly once, then said: if we go for the full date, I'm all in. Disagree and commit.
The director chose the phased plan — and I owned the delivery of it.

props.learning: Bring an alternative, not just an objection. And mean the commit.
props.foot: A spine and professional maturity in one answer — exactly what managing up needs.

props.title: Influence without authority
props.q: How did you drive a decision across teams you don't own?

moves.title: Name the stakeholders
moves.desc: Who cared, what they wanted, where incentives clashed.

moves.title: Sell the why
moves.desc: Build a shared narrative plus data, so it becomes their idea too.

moves.title: Trade and align
moves.desc: Find the win-win; give something to get the alignment you need.

moves.title: Land it, credit others
moves.desc: Show the decision shipped, and spread the credit widely.

props.trap: You “escalated to your VP.” That's borrowing authority, not influence.
props.signal: You can move an org through persuasion, the core senior-EM muscle.
props.foot: The higher the role, the more your power is influence, not your title.

props.title: Three teams, three feature-flag systems, no authority
props.situation: Three teams had each built their own feature-flag system. It was wasteful, inconsistent, and had caused two incidents. Nobody owned consolidation, and I had zero authority over the other two teams.
props.task: My mandate — self-assigned: get all three onto one platform.

actions.d: Mapped the stakeholders and their incentives — one team cared about speed, one about safety, one about cost.
Built a shared proposal and a small working prototype that solved each team's single biggest pain point.
Traded: I offered to have my team own and staff the platform, if they adopted it.
Landed it in an architecture review, and credited the other teams' input publicly.

props.learning: Influence is finding the win-win, then doing the unglamorous integration work yourself.
props.foot: You moved an org through persuasion, not your title. That's the senior-EM muscle.

props.title: Delivery
A project that missed its deadline
props.q: Tell me about a project that slipped or missed a deadline.

moves.title: Own it plainly
moves.desc: No blaming QA, the PM, or “requirements changed.”

moves.title: Detect it early
moves.desc: How you saw the slip coming and re-planned, not last minute.

moves.title: Communicate up early
moves.desc: You raised the risk and options before it blew up.

moves.title: Fix the system
moves.desc: What you changed so it can't recur: estimation, scope, staffing.

props.trap: A blameless story where nothing was your fault and you learned nothing.
props.signal: You surface bad news early and turn a miss into a durable fix.
props.foot: How you handle a slip matters more than the slip itself.

props.title: The launch that was going to miss by two months
props.situation: We'd committed a major search-relevance launch to the org for the third quarter. Six weeks out, a core dependency team slipped, and it was clear we were going to miss badly.
props.task: My mandate: recover the situation, not just the date.

actions.d: Caught it early — our burn-down stopped adding up, so I flagged it six weeks out, not the week before.
Re-planned with the team: cut two non-critical features and parallelized the critical path.
Communicated up immediately — the risk, the new plan, and the trade-offs — before anyone asked.
Set a weekly exec update so leadership was never surprised again.

props.learning: The miss is survivable. Hiding it is not. Escalate early, with a plan.
props.foot: You turned a slip into a controlled, communicated recovery. That's what they want.

props.title: A hard trade-off, or saying no
props.q: Tell me about a hard trade-off, or a time you said no.

moves.title: Frame the tension
moves.desc: Speed versus quality; a feature versus paying down debt.

moves.title: Make criteria explicit
moves.desc: Decide on principles and data, not the loudest voice.

moves.title: Say no with a reason
moves.desc: Decline clearly, explain the why, offer an alternative.

moves.title: Stand by it
moves.desc: Show the outcome, and that you'd defend the call again.

props.trap: You tried to please everyone, so nothing was actually prioritized.
props.signal: You can prioritize under pressure and hold the line when it's right.
props.foot: Managers who can't say no ship blurry roadmaps and burned-out teams.

props.title: Saying no to the biggest customer
props.situation: Our largest enterprise customer demanded a custom reporting feature, and sales was pushing hard. Meanwhile, reliability debt had caused three incidents that quarter and was threatening our SLA.
props.task: My mandate: decide where the team's next quarter actually goes.

actions.d: Made the criteria explicit — I laid out the cost of the incidents in churn risk versus the value of one deal.
Took it to data: one customer's request, versus SLA breaches affecting hundreds of accounts.
Said no to the custom feature, clearly, with the reasoning — and offered a lighter alternative on the standard roadmap.
Held the line with sales and my VP, and put the quarter on reliability.

props.learning: Saying no with a reason and an alternative builds more trust than a reluctant yes.
props.foot: You prioritized under real pressure and held the line. That's the judgment they test.

props.title: Leading through an incident
props.q: Walk me through a major outage you led through.

moves.title: Set the stakes fast
moves.desc: Impact in one line: users, revenue, duration. Then move on.

moves.title: Lead calm, coordinate
moves.desc: You ran the response, roles and comms, not solo heroics.

moves.title: Communicate outward
moves.desc: Honest, frequent updates to stakeholders during the fire.

moves.title: Blameless postmortem
moves.desc: The real leadership: the fix that makes a repeat impossible.

props.trap: You personally fixed it at 3am. Heroic, but you led no one.
props.signal: You're the calm center in a crisis, and you build systems, not patches.
props.foot: In an incident they watch one thing: does the room calm down when you speak?

props.title: Checkout down on Black Friday
props.situation: On Black Friday, checkout started failing. A payment-provider integration degraded, and about fifteen percent of transactions were erroring. We were bleeding revenue by the minute.
props.task: My mandate: lead the response — as the manager, not the debugger.

actions.d: Set stakes and structure fast — declared a Sev-1, took incident-commander, assigned a comms lead and a debug lead. I did not touch the code.
Ran one clear channel and updated stakeholders honestly every fifteen minutes.
We failed over to the backup provider within forty minutes to stop the bleeding, then root-caused calmly.
Ran a blameless postmortem; the durable fix was an automatic circuit-breaker and failover.

props.learning: In a crisis, your job is to coordinate and communicate — not to be the hero.
props.foot: Calm center, honest comms, systemic fix. That's the leadership they're scanning for.

props.title: Scale & Self
Building and scaling a team
props.q: Tell me about a time you built or scaled a team.

moves.title: Hire to a bar
moves.desc: Define the bar and raise it. Who you said no to, not just yes.

moves.title: Build for diversity
moves.desc: Widen the funnel and structure interviews to reduce bias.

moves.title: Onboard for impact
moves.desc: How new hires reached real output fast, ramp not sink-or-swim.

moves.title: Show the health
moves.desc: Retention, velocity, promotions. The team outlived the hiring.

props.trap: “I hired ten people.” Headcount is not a skill; the bar is.
props.signal: You build durable teams, not just bigger ones.
props.foot: Senior signal: you scale the org, and the quality bar goes up, not down.

props.title: From four engineers to twenty in a year
props.situation: We got funding to grow a new infrastructure team from four engineers to twenty in a year. I owned the hiring bar and the culture, under real pressure to just fill seats fast.
props.task: My mandate: scale fast without dropping the bar or building a monoculture.

actions.d: Defined the bar explicitly and trained every interviewer — and I personally reviewed the rejections, not just the offers.
Widened the funnel deliberately: partnered with programs for underrepresented candidates and used structured interviews to cut bias.
Built real onboarding — a 30-60-90 plan and a buddy — so new hires shipped in weeks, not months.
Protected the culture with explicit values and fast, early feedback for every new hire.

props.learning: Headcount is easy. A high bar and a healthy culture at speed is the actual job.
props.foot: You scaled the org and the bar went up, not down. That's the senior signal.

props.title: Acting with no direction
props.q: Tell me about a time you acted with no clear direction.

moves.title: Name the fog
moves.desc: No spec, no owner, unclear goal. Be honest about the ambiguity.

moves.title: Create the clarity
moves.desc: You wrote the doc, set the goal, drew the line to follow.

moves.title: Make a reversible bet
moves.desc: Pick a direction, ship small, learn. Don't wait for permission.

moves.title: Bring people with you
moves.desc: You aligned the team around the clarity you manufactured.

props.trap: You waited for someone above you to tell you what to do.
props.signal: You generate direction instead of consuming it. The leap into leadership.
props.foot: The more senior the role, the more the job IS the ambiguity.

props.title: “Developer productivity is too low” — go fix it
props.situation: My VP said, “developer productivity is too low,” and handed it to me. No spec, no metric, no team. Just a vague, politically charged problem and an expectation that I'd figure it out.
props.task: My mandate: turn a complaint into an actual direction.

actions.d: Named the ambiguity and created clarity — I interviewed thirty engineers and instrumented our build and CI pipeline to find the real bottlenecks.
Wrote a one-page strategy with a single north-star metric: time from commit to production.
Made a reversible bet — started with the biggest bottleneck, flaky tests, and shipped a fix in three weeks to show a win.
Aligned the org around the one-pager and pulled together a small team to go further.

props.learning: Leaders manufacture direction out of ambiguity instead of waiting for a spec.
props.foot: You generated direction where there was none. That's the leap into real leadership.

props.title: Your biggest failure
props.q: What's the biggest failure of your career?

moves.title: Pick a real one
moves.desc: A genuine failure with real cost, not “I work too hard.”

moves.title: Own your part fully
moves.desc: Your decisions and their consequences. Don't diffuse blame.

moves.title: Extract the lesson
moves.desc: The specific principle you now operate by because of it.

moves.title: Prove it changed you
moves.desc: A later time you did it differently, and it worked.

props.trap: A humblebrag disguised as a failure. Interviewers spot it instantly.
props.signal: You're self-aware, accountable, and you genuinely learn.
props.foot: This is the most important story you'll tell. Have a real one.

props.title: The person I kept too long
props.situation: Early as a manager, I had an engineer who was quietly underperforming. I liked him, so I gave him “one more quarter” — three times, across a whole year. This is a real mistake I own.
props.task: The honest version: I avoided a hard conversation and told myself it was kindness.

actions.d: Own it plainly: I dodged the hard conversation because it was uncomfortable, and I dressed it up as being kind.
The real cost: two of my strongest engineers burned out covering for him, and one of them left the company.
The lesson: tolerating underperformance isn't kindness to anyone — it's a tax on your best people.
How I changed: the next time, I gave clear feedback and a firm 60-day plan in week one, and acted when it didn't close.

metrics.l: my rule now, not a year

props.learning: Avoiding a hard conversation is a decision — and it's usually the wrong one.
props.foot: A real failure, fully owned, with proof you changed. That's the maturity test, passed.

items: It's one question: how do you lead when it's hard?
Structure every answer with STAR, plus the Learning.
Say “I” for your decisions; give the team the credit.
Two sentences of context, then live in the Action.
End on a measurable result, and what you learned.
Prep 12 to 15 real stories in a category matrix.
props.closer: They're not testing what you did. They're testing how you think.
